title: brandpositioningstatementexample
claim: A positioning statement is useless unless it explicitly names what the brand chooses to give up.
hook: Every standard brand positioning statement example misses the one thing that makes strategy work: explicit trade-offs.

slides.headline: Why your positioning statement does not work
The textbook formula creates generic positioning
slides.body: For urban commuters who need clean transit Ather is the electric scooter that offers smart features. This sounds logical but it gives up nothing.

slides.headline: Real positioning requires an explicit trade-off
slides.body: Strategy is not deciding what to say. It is deciding what customers to alienate so your core audience believes you completely.

slides.headline: How to rewrite the classic positioning formula
slides.body: Instead of listing benefits, state what you deliberately sacrifice. If your competitor cannot claim the exact opposite, your positioning is useless.

slides.headline: Compare these two positioning statements
slides.body: Weak: Premium performance for modern commuters. Sharp: We built a high-priced software machine, not a cheap utility scooter.

slides.headline: Test your strategy before writing copy
slides.body: Ask your team: What customer segment are we actively choosing to lose? If the answer is no one, your positioning statement is just wishful thinking.

slides.headline: Send this to your brand lead
slides.body: Forward this carousel to someone currently writing a positioning deck before they sign off on generic benefits.

caption:
Every standard brand positioning statement example misses the one thing that makes strategy work: explicit trade-offs.

Most positioning templates follow the classic formula: For [target audience] who [need], [brand] is the [category] that [key benefit].

The problem with this template is that it allows brand teams to list positive adjectives without making a hard choice. When Ather launched in India, they did not position themselves as an electric scooter for commuters. They built a high-priced, software-driven vehicle and accepted losing the mass price-sensitive market entirely.

If your competitor cannot take the exact opposite stance without sounding irrational, you have not positioned your brand. You have just written a wish list.

Real brand strategy is defined by what you choose to sacrifice.

Forward this to a marketer who is writing positioning copy this week.
